title: How to Create High End Coaching Solutions
overview: Ajit Nawalkha, co-founder of Mindvalley Coach and author of The Book of Coaching and Live Big, closed Day 2 with a 25-minute answer to why some experts can only charge a few hundred dollars while others charge six figures for what looks like the same expertise. You learned his CARES method, the difference between solving for pain and solving for gain, and exactly which elements a $3,000, $30,000 and $100,000-plus offer each need. He asked you to sit with the model for 30 to 60 minutes and find the one gap to fix next, and noted that the Expert to Authority Mastery programme is designed to help fill those gaps.
key_ideas: A high-ticket offer is anything over $3,000, and the same approach Ajit teaches here has generated over $57 million in certifications since 2022 (the business grew so strongly that Mindvalley asked to partner, which is how it became Mindvalley Coach). In parallel this year his digital products have reached over 2,000 students and $453,000, and a Dubai-only consulting and AI offer made $160,000 in its first 60 days. He built all of this while keeping a promise, made when his first child arrived, to work no more than five or six hours a day.

Nobody buys your package; everybody buys your result. Early in his coaching career Ajit packed offers with calls and hours, and even clients who signed up would say a few weeks later 'but I signed up for the thing all this was supposed to give me'. The only question for what goes into a product is whether it moves the client toward the result.

Solving for pain versus solving for gain decides your price. Pain (lose five or ten pounds) is how you make some money, but it is a highly competitive market where someone always undercuts you, a race to the bottom. Gain serves people who are already successful and want the next level: deeper in an already good relationship, another million on an existing business. It is harder to sell but has far less competition and much higher prices. Anything over $3,000 usually has to be solving for gain: you take someone who is already good and make them great.

The CARES method is the five letters to remember when designing a higher-tier programme: Convenient (how easy is it to access you and the programme), Affinity (how close and accessible you are to this group), Return on investment (can you justify the dollars going in), Exclusive (10 people or 5,000; the less exclusive, the less expensive) and Status, the secret one: how does the client feel saying 'my coach is ___'. Status defines the highest fee you can charge.

Each price tier leans on different CARES elements. A $3,000 training mostly sells convenience: online, recordings, some AI support, enrolment once or twice a year, tied to a direct result. At $30,000 the buyer wants return on investment; they typically earn $300,000 to $400,000 or have disposable income from a job, exit or investments, and they need the fear of that spend justified. From $30,000 to $40,000 up to $100,000 you must add exclusivity and affinity: are you taking a few clients or thousands, and do I get real access to you. Ajit runs $3,000 trainings, $30,000 consulting programmes, $40,000 AI-plus-consulting programmes and a $150,000-a-year private tier for a handful of clients.

Above $100,000 it is almost entirely about status. At $3,000 and even $30,000 it is all about results, but at $100,000 to $150,000 the question is whether you are the authority in that field. People who charge in this range invest very heavily in social media, funnels and advertising because they want the client to walk in already convinced; they have experienced you across social, webinars and funnels and built a whole world around you.

Authority removes the convincing. Enrolment is the hardest part of most coaching and consulting businesses because it is a tedious convincing process. When you are an authority the person arrives asking only for the details: that you are not over-enrolling, that they can trust you, and that they will get results. Blending all five CARES elements makes enrolment easier and also makes it easier to create results with the clients you take on.

Use the theory of constraints to choose your next move: find the one big thing that acts like a domino for your whole business. Earlier this year Ajit's newer business, Greater Insight, had great products and loyal clients but was not growing fast enough; the constraint was leads. He found the two reasons, fixed them, and the business has grown 100 percent every month for the last three months. Information without action changes nothing, so the one gap you identify is what to work on next.

frameworks.name: The CARES method
steps: C is for Convenient: how easy is it to access the programme and to work with you
A is for Affinity: how close you are to this group and how much access they have to you
R is for Return on investment: can you justify that the money going in comes back
E is for Exclusive: is it limited to 10, 50, 500 people; the less exclusive, the less expensive
S is for Status: how the client feels associating with you when they say 'my coach is ___'; this sets the highest fee you can charge

frameworks.name: Solving for pain versus solving for gain
steps: Solving for pain (lose five pounds, fix a problem) makes some money but puts you in a crowded market where price is a race to the bottom
Solving for gain (taking someone already successful to the next level) is harder to sell but has less competition and much higher prices
Any offer over $3,000 usually has to solve for gain: you take somebody who is already good and make them great

frameworks.name: What each price tier needs (as Ajit laid it out)
steps: $3,000: convenience plus a direct result; online, recordings, some AI, enrolment once or twice a year
$30,000: return on investment; the buyer usually earns $300,000 to $400,000 or has disposable income and needs the spend justified
$30,000 to $40,000 up to $100,000: convenience and ROI plus exclusivity (few clients) and affinity (real access to you)
$100,000 to $150,000 and above: status; the client sees you as the authority and walks in already convinced

frameworks.name: Theory of constraints, as Ajit applies it
steps: Ask: what is the one big thing that, if fixed, acts like a domino for the whole business
Find out why that thing is not yet solved (for his Greater Insight business it was leads, with two specific causes)
Fix those causes and measure the change

exercises: Type the CARES letters you already have in your business today (Convenient, Affinity, Return on investment, Exclusive, Status) and notice which are missing.
Answer honestly: why should a client sign with you? Why should they trust you? Why should they want to work with you?

Take a 30- to 60-minute block, sit with all the models you wrote down over the two days, including CARES, and check whether your current offer fits. Where it does not, write down what needs to change, what you need to learn, what you need to engage with and what community you need to be part of. Writing it down makes your next move obvious.
next_steps: Score your main offer against each CARES letter and pick the single missing element to add first.
Decide whether your offer is solving for pain or for gain; if you want to price above $3,000, rewrite the promised result for someone who is already good and wants to be great.
Choose the tier you are aiming for ($3,000, $30,000, or $100,000-plus) and list the specific elements that tier requires: convenience, ROI proof, exclusivity and access, or visible status.
Apply the theory of constraints: name the one domino holding your business back this quarter, find the reasons behind it and fix those first.
attribution_notes: Lines labelled with Ajit Nawalkha's name were attributed to him (the transcript introduction spelt it 'Ajid Nawaka'); lines labelled 'Mindvalley' were the host Jason Goldberg's introduction, recap of the day and sign-off; there was no host question-and-answer with the speaker.
